title: Question 9
statement_text: Is the upper bound of $\frac{n}{\sqrt{2k}}$ on the number of $k$-planar subgraphs needed to partition the complete convex geometric graph $K(P)$ on $n$ points (more precisely, a partition into $\lceil\frac{n}{s}\rceil$ $\frac{(s-1)(s-2)}{2}$-planar subgraphs for every $s>2$) tight up to lower-order terms?
context_text: A geometric graph is a drawing of a graph in the plane with vertices at points in general position and edges as straight-line segments; two edges cross if they share a point in their relative interiors, and a geometric graph is $k$-planar (or $k$-plane) if each edge crosses at most $k$ other edges. For a point set $P$, $K(P)$ is the complete geometric graph on $P$, and a $k$-planar partition of $K(P)$ is a partition of its edges into $k$-planar subgraphs (an edge coloring in which each color class is $k$-planar); $P$ is in convex position here. The authors prove that for $n$ points in convex position, $K(P)$ admits a partition into at most $\frac{n}{\sqrt{2k}}$ $k$-planar subgraphs, obtained by grouping the $n$ edge slopes of a regular $n$-gon into $\lceil n/s\rceil$ circular intervals of size $s$, which gives $\frac{(s-1)(s-2)}{2}$-planar classes; conversely, using an improved crossing lemma for convex geometric graphs, at least $\frac{n-1}{4.93\sqrt{k}}$ subgraphs are required. For $k=1$ they prove the tight bound $\lceil n/3\rceil$ (for $n\ge5$). They ask in particular whether, when $k$ is far from $\frac{(s-1)(s-2)}{2}$, one can improve on $\lceil n/s\rceil$, and find this question surprisingly difficult; for $k=2$ they can show, with computer assistance, a lower bound of $\frac{3n}{10}$, almost matching the upper bound $\frac{n}{3}$, but omit this result from this version.
paper_title: Edge Partitions of Complete Geometric Graphs (Part 2)
